items.prose: A 10% trimmed mean cuts 10% of the data from each end.
items.question: What is its breakdown point?

widget.accept: 10%: up to 10% at one end can be moved without moving the estimate past bounds.
widget.label: Breakdown point

feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many values at one end can be trimmed away?

byKey.both: 20% are cut in all, but only 10% at each end: 11% at one end break it.

explain.text: If more than 10% of the data go to one extreme, some survive the trim and drag the mean. So the breakdown point is 10%.

items.prose: One day of a strategy's 60 is replaced by a 30% gain.
items.question: Which pair of summaries moves the most?

options.text: The mean and the standard deviation

options.why: Both have breakdown point one half; one day barely moves them.

options.text: The ranks of the other days
options.why: Only that day's rank changes, to 60.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which summaries use every value's size?

explain.text: The mean and SD use sizes, so one day moves them without limit; the median, MAD and ranks do not.

items.prose: Lesson 9's experiment paired two algorithms within 200 stock-days, and the shortfall noise had fat tails.
items.question: Which rank test suits it?

options.text: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the 200 within-day differences
Mann-Whitney on the 200 A orders against the 200 B orders
options.why: That ignores the pairing, like the unpaired $t$-test.
The sign test is valid but throws away the sizes; signed ranks keep their order.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the pairs.

explain.text: The design was paired, so test the differences. The signed-rank test gave 0.00484, between the sign test's 0.0194 and the $t$-test's 0.00579.

items.prose: A sign-flip test checks whether a strategy's mean daily P&L is 0.
items.question: What does flipping signs assume under the null?

options.text: That each day's P&L is symmetric about 0

options.why: Symmetry is enough; normality is not needed.
It needs symmetry about 0, and independent days.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. When are $x$ and $-x$ equally likely?

explain.text: If each day is symmetric about 0 and independent, every sign pattern is equally likely. A skewed P&L breaks that.
